title: Handle and store fuel safely
summary: Petrol, diesel and propane are among the first supplies looted and the most dangerous to handle. Move fuel with a pump, never your mouth; store it outdoors in proper containers; keep sparks and static away; and learn to spot fuel that has gone bad.

materials.item: Hand transfer pump or self-priming siphon hose
Proper fuel cans with tight caps
Funnel and a clean cloth or filter
Clear glass jar for checking fuel
Fire extinguisher, bucket of sand or fire blanket
Soapy water in a spray bottle, for gas leak checks

steps.text: Work outdoors, upwind, away from flames, running engines and anyone smoking. Have the extinguisher or sand ready.

Check fuel before you take it. Pour a little into a clear jar and let it settle. Good petrol is clear and light. Stale petrol is darker and smells sour or like varnish. Water and sludge sink to the bottom as a separate layer.
Move fuel with a hand pump or a self-priming siphon. Many newer cars have a valve or screen that stops a hose reaching the tank; don't force it.
steps.warn: Never start a siphon by mouth. Fuel in the lungs causes a severe pneumonia that can kill.

steps.text: At petrol stations, the underground tanks have fill points under round covers on the forecourt. Pump from them with a long hose and a hand pump, keeping the end of the hose clear of the bottom so you don't pull up water and sludge.
steps.warn: Tank openings hold heavy vapour. No sparks, and don't put your face over the opening.

steps.text: Put cans on the ground to fill them, never in a vehicle or on a plastic liner. Keep the nozzle touching the can so static can't spark.
Leave a little space at the top of each can for expansion, close it tightly and wipe off spills.
Store fuel in a shaded, ventilated shed or outdoor store, away from living spaces, wells and streams.
Keep propane cylinders upright and outdoors, with the valve closed when not in use. Check every connection with soapy water: growing bubbles mean a leak.
steps.warn: Propane is heavier than air and pools in basements, pits and low ground.

steps.text: Let engines cool before refuelling. Never refuel a running engine or a hot generator.
steps.warn: Petrol spilled on a hot exhaust can ignite.

steps.text: Use the oldest fuel first. Add stabiliser to fresh fuel if you have it, and label cans with the date.

notes:
## Shelf life

| Fuel | Rough life, sealed and cool | Signs it has gone off |
|---|---|---|
| Petrol with ethanol | about 3–6 months; longer with stabiliser | darker, sour or varnish smell, water layer, hard starting |
| Petrol without ethanol | longer, perhaps a year | same |
| Diesel | about 6–12 months; longer with stabiliser and biocide | dark, cloudy, slime or sludge at the bottom |
| Kerosene (paraffin) | years if sealed and dry | cloudy, water at the bottom |
| Propane | indefinitely in a sound cylinder | rusty, dented or damaged cylinder |

These are rough. Heat, air and water shorten them.

## Vapour

Petrol vapour burns at only about 1–8% in air, so a small spill in a closed room can be enough. The vapour is heavier than air and flows downhill along floors to pilot lights, heaters and switches.

## Static

Fuel flowing through a hose builds static charge. A can sitting on a plastic truck bed liner or carpet can't let the charge go, and it sparks at the nozzle. On the ground, the charge drains away.

## Wrong fuel

- Petrol in a diesel engine can wreck it.
- Diesel in a petrol engine stops it running.
- Two-stroke engines (chainsaws, trimmers, many outboards) need oil mixed into the petrol. The ratio is usually on the tank cap or in the manual.

## Common mistakes

- Filling cans in a truck bed.
- Storing a fuel can inside the house.
- Using petrol to start a fire.
- Topping up a hot generator.
- Storing propane in a basement or tent.
